title: The ULTIMATE Cardio/Calves Exercises Tier-List
summary: Final episode of NH's exercise tier-list series: about 40 cardio options ranked for bodybuilders (calorie burn, fatigue, time cost, tendon impact), followed by a calf exercise tier list based on loadability, stretch, slow tempo and isolation. He argues cardio improves work capacity and recovery, that calves are not purely genetic but need heavy load and lots of volume, and that the best exercise is the one you will stick to.
claims: Cardio is ranked for bodybuilding conditioning (calories, fatigue, time, tendon impact), not sport performance
Being big, lean or vascular does not mean being fit; heart and lung fitness is separate from hypertrophy
Good cardio does not kill gains; it boosts them through better work capacity (more volume), better pumps and faster recovery
Walking is B tier: very low impact and low fatigue but time-consuming (10,000-20,000 steps)
Running is C tier because it taxes lower back, shins and knees and can interfere with leg training
Long-distance running is D tier: it requires losing muscle mass and is too demanding in time and energy
Sprinting is A tier: short and intense, 1-2 times a week is already a lot, but it carries hamstring strain risk so warm up and do weighted stretches
Joggers typically need to run 3-4 times a week to benefit
Fartlek (jog 1-2 min, sprint about 10 s, repeat) is S tier; NH has practised it for a long time
Rebounding on a trampoline is S tier: about as intense as jogging with no tendon impact, good for the lymphatic system, 15-50 minutes a day at home
The treadmill is D tier: it does part of the work for you so 10,000 steps on it are far easier than outside
Jump rope is a poor cardio choice for bodybuilders: high coordination cost and low taxation once learned
Jumping jacks are B tier: no coordination or equipment needed
Burpees are A tier: full-body, very breathless, build some muscle
The rowing machine is S tier: big back and leg muscles, little knee and shoulder impact, very time-efficient if done properly
AMRAP sets on compounds (e.g., 30-40 rep squats) are C tier: stopped by heart and lungs, taxing on joints, use sparingly
Giant sets are B tier: passive cardio with almost no cost if not turned into a circuit
After 4 years of giant sets and no dedicated cardio he found his cardiovascular endurance well preserved, helped by an athletics background
HIIT as a method is A tier: spiking heart rate then lower intensity is very beneficial for health and fat loss
Swimming is A tier: low impact, fun, builds shoulders and back; less than 15 minutes of sprint intervals will spend you; shoulder injuries possible
Aqua aerobics done hard by a fit person is S tier, and he rehabbed a knee injury in the pool with it
Battle ropes are C tier because shoulder endurance gives out before heart and lungs
Medicine ball slams are B tier: rotational training for athletes, not ideal for bodybuilders
Kettlebell training is A tier: versatile, easy on joints, high reps, builds muscle
Sandbag training is S tier: cheap DIY implement, versatile and very hard
Mountain climbers are C tier: decent ab and cardio work but chest and shoulders give out first
Vertical climber machine is B tier; rope climbing is A tier and reveals strength-to-weight weaknesses like grip and back
Jacob's ladder is A tier but the machine costs about $6,000
StairMaster is S tier, the best cardio machine; used at high pace you won't last over 20 minutes; half bodyweight in a backpack for 10 minutes makes you a cardio monster
Climbing real stairs is B tier: falls, the descent, slippery steps
Crawling is S tier: challenges the whole body and lungs, no equipment
Under-desk steppers are D tier and do nothing
Stationary exercise bikes are C tier, elliptical B tier, air (assault) bike A tier
Outdoor biking is S tier: 10 minutes up a hill is a great workout and also works calves
Alpine skiing is D tier: high rate of knee ligament injuries and expensive; cross-country skiing is B tier
Snowshoeing is A tier: builds stamina and big legs but is hard on knee ligaments
Hiking is A tier: uneven terrain conditions ankles, knees and lower back
Rucking (weighted backpack walk) is S tier; 15-30 minutes under heavy load builds posture and comfort under heavy weights
Wood chopping is A tier: back, shoulders, mobility and explosiveness
Cardio-heavy movements usually recruit calves poorly
Calves are not 100% genetic; people fail due to inconsistency and poor exercise selection
A good calf exercise is easy to load and progress, allows a deep stretch, needs little balance or cardio, and allows slow tempo to protect the Achilles
Bodyweight calf raises are D tier because calves already do that daily when walking
Donkey calf raises are C tier: hard to load, stress the lower back, target nothing special
Seated calf raises are B tier: big stretch and you can push on the weight in the stretch beyond failure, but strong position and knee pad discomfort
Standing variations activate more of the calf than seated per recent studies; do both
Single-leg calf raise is A tier: fixes side imbalances and ankle flexibility but is hard to load
Standing two-leg calf raise is S tier with foot elevated, slow tempo, high reps and progressive load; machine or Smith rather than barbell
Dumbbell calf hops are D tier: poor stretch, bad tempo, low load
Plyometrics are D tier for calves: power comes from knees and hips; he could dunk but had poor calves
Running and jump rope are C tier for calves: burn is not growth
Biking is B tier for calves if set up so the heel comes off the pedal
Being fat grows calves because they carry extra load all day, the lesson being more load equals bigger calves
Weighted StairMaster on tiptoes with a backpack is S tier for calves
Calves are resilient and need much more volume; 6 sets a week is almost nothing
Squats do not grow calves (D tier): many naturals have big quads and no calves, including him
Squat jumps C tier; power cleans B tier for calves
Tiptoe farmer's walk is A tier for calves: 4-5 minutes with straps, but taxing
Calf press on the leg press is S tier: great tension, easy to superset and do several times a week
Tibialis raise is C tier: great for shin splint rehab
Calf launcher (Nordic-style calf exercise) is B tier
Sled push is a fun calf builder because the heels come off the floor; strongmen have big calves
Ballerinas have huge calves from staying on tiptoes
The best exercise is the one you'll stick to: pick enjoyable S/A options and do them several times a week for a year
exercises: pull with back, drive with legs
foot elevated, slow tempo, high reps, machine or Smith
push on the weight at stretch end of set
